---
title: Inflatables Report 8/6/2019
---

We now have a full pipeline in place to construct an inflatable sheet for a
target 3D surface and simulate its deployment. This pipeline consists of:

1. Parametrization: flattening the target 3D surface to the plane with a mapping
   that emulates the behavior of the inflating air channels.
2. Constructing air channel walls that align well with the directions extracted
   from the parametrization.
3. Simulating the inflation of these air channels.

This report describes the algorithm for constructing air channels and then
discusses some alterations to the parametrization stage [proposed in the last report](4_10_2019.html#formulation){target=".blank"}
that were needed to obtain reasonable results.

## Air Channel Construction

We take the piecewise linear parametrization $f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}^2$
of our triangulated target surface $\mathcal{M}$ and compute the SVD of its
(constant) Jacobian on each triangle,
$$
    \nabla f = U
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \sigma_0 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & \sigma_1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    V^T,
\label{eqn:svd}\tag{1}
$$
where $U = \left({\bf u}_0\, {\bf u}_1\right)$
and $V = \left({\bf v}_0\,  {\bf v}_1 \, {\bf n} \right)$ are matrices holding the
left and right singular vectors in their columns. The singular values are
sorted in descending order, so singular vectors ${\bf u}_0$ and ${\bf v}_0$ are
the material directions in 2D and 3D along which lengths are stretched by the
flattening ($\sigma_0 \approx \frac{\pi}{2}$). Singular vectors ${\bf u}_1$ and
${\bf v}_1$ are the directions along which the mapping preserves lengths
($\sigma_1 \approx 1.0$), i.e., the implied channel orientations. Finally,
the third right singular vector ${\bf n}$ is the triangle's normal.

We use the algorithm from @Knoppel2015 to construct a stripe pattern aligned
with ${\bf u}_1$ (in the pane). We subdivide the flat 2D triangle mesh $f(\mathcal{M})$
to give the stripe pattern algorithm greater resolution to work with and smooth the per-triangle orientation
field ${\bf u}_1$ into per-vertex 2D angles as required by the algorithm (using a
circular mean to average the angles). We also specify a spatial frequency, which controls
the scale of the air channels (increasing this parameter packs more air channels into the sheet).
The resulting stripe field is then sampled on an even finer subdivided triangle mesh.

The "stripe field" is effectively a distance field to the channel
wall centers in scaled/nondimensionalized units: the field is 0 at the wall center and
increases at an approximately constant rate as you move perpendicularly to the wall. The field
reaches a peak value of $\pi$ at the channel center before dropping back to $0$ at the next wall center
(the spacing between wall centers is always $2 \pi$ in these scaled units):

![Figure 1: Example stripe field for the Lilium tower model.](images/stripe_field.png){width=600px}

Recall that the channel wall width adjusts the amount of contraction induced by channel inflation.
So for a given parametrization $f$, we must choose the wall widths according to the stretch $\sigma_0$ that $f$
applies when flattening the target surface to the plane.
For instance, if $\sigma_0$ is the maximum value of $\frac{\pi}{2}$,
then the walls must have zero width so that the air channels occupy the full
span of $2 \pi$ units between their walls. For a general, spatially varying
$\sigma_0,$ the formula for wall widths in our nondimensionalized units is:
$$
w = \frac{\frac{2 \pi}{\sigma_0} - 4}{1 - \frac{2}{\pi}}.
$$

Subtracting this scalar field $w$ will shift the stripe field so that its
zero contour curves lie at distance $w$ from the wall center. In other
words, the zero contours of the shifted stripe field are now exactly where we
need to draw wall boundaries; I extract these contours as polylines and then simplify
them by uniformly resampling at a specified arc length increment (otherwise they
are very high resolution and noisy).

![Figure 2: Extracted walls for the Lilium tower model.](images/extracted_walls.png){width=600px}

Finally, I construct a Delaunay triangulation of the flattened mesh that
contains these wall polylines. The triangulation library I use,
[Triangle](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~quake/triangle.html), can track which
vertices of the output mesh originate from the input wall polylines; these wall
vertices are used to fuse the top and bottom sheets together for simulation.

## Attempting Inflation

With the inflation sheet mesh thus constructed, we can now attempt the
inflation simulation to see how well the design works.
Unfortunately, even if we "cheat" by forcing the sheet onto the target surface as
an initialization for the equilibrium solver (lifting the mesh to 3D by
applying $f^{-1}$ to its vertices), the sheet immediately pops into a very
different shape:

### Metric Validation
This behavior is not due to a failure of the parametrization $f$ to properly encode the
target shape as a new metric on 2D sheet $D := f(\mathcal{M}) \subset \mathbb{R}^2$.
In fact, we can verify that the metric encodes our shape by solving the
following minimization problem for an immersion $h : D \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with
the metric used to design the air channels:
$$
\min_h \frac{1}{2} \int_D \! \|\nabla \mathcal{h}^T \nabla \mathcal{h} - g\|_F^2 \, \mathrm{d}A + E_\text{shell}(h),
\label{eqn:metric_fit}\tag{2}
$$
where $g = {\bf u}_1 \otimes {\bf u}_1 + \frac{1}{\texttt{clamp}(\sigma_0)} {\bf u}_0 \otimes  {\bf u}_0$
is the metric taken from $f$ after clamping to the $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_1$ values permitted by
the air channel mechanism, and $E_\text{shell}$ is a bending regularization energy based on the dihedral
angles between triangles introduced in @Grinspun2003. Solving $(\ref{eqn:metric_fit})$ reproduces
the qualitative features of the Lilium tower surface (click to play):
<figure>
<video height="400px" width="600px" onclick="this.paused ? this.play() : this.pause();" playsinline>
    <source src="videos/metric_fitting_free_bdry.mov" type="video/mp4">
</video>
</figure>
The reproduction is even better if we apply a Dirichlet boundary condition
gluing the boundary $\partial D$ to the target surface's boundary curve while solving
$(\ref{eqn:metric_fit})$:
<figure>
<video height="400px" width="600px" onclick="this.paused ? this.play() : this.pause();" playsinline>
    <source src="videos/metric_fitting_fixed_bdry.mov" type="video/mp4">
</video>
</figure>
This improvement when fixing the boundary is expected since shells become much
more rigid when their boundaries are constrained; if we free the boundary to
deform, we can find many different shapes that are nearly isometric to the
original.

Incidentally, we can use this metric fitting approach to reconstruct the
theoretical shape of the [concentric circles](4_10_2019.html#concentric-circles) design:
<figure>
<video height="400px" width="600px" onclick="this.paused ? this.play() : this.pause();" playsinline>
    <source src="videos/negative_cone.mov" type="video/mp4">
</video>
</figure>
Note that the shape has all of its Gaussian curvature concentrated at a
singularity in the center, and the surface is developable away from the center
(i.e., it is truly a negative cone). The inflated counterpart smoothes this negative
curvature across more of the surface--and has a less extreme cone angle.

## New Regularization Term

We can understand why the inflation fails to produce the correct shape even
when the encoded metric appears to be good by studying the inflation in Figure
3 more carefully. Apparently the issue is that the long air channels spanning
across the shape must bend significantly to fit to the surface, but inflation
forces the tubes to straighten out. We need to modify our parametrization
algorithm to consider more than just the in-plane metric-changing effects of the
air channels; it must ensure the air channels bend as little as possible in
their deployed configuration to mitigate the effects of straightening.

To this end, we develop a "homogenized" anisotropic bending energy model to
capture the reluctance of the inflated tubes to bend. We base our model
on a standard bending energy used for beams and rods:
$$\frac{1}{2} \int \! \kappa^2 \, \mathrm{d}s,$$
where $\kappa$ is the curvature
of the beam's centerline. Imagine the area element $\mathrm{d}A$ at a point ${\bf x}$ on our
surface $\mathcal{M}$ is filled with many parallel inflated tubes all oriented in
direction ${\bf v}_1$ (i.e., the channel directions implied by the parametrization $f$).
Summing the bending energy over all the segments of tubes fitting inside $\mathrm{d}A$ gives
us an energy proportional to $\kappa({\bf v}_1)^2 \mathrm{d}A$, where $\kappa({\bf v}_1)$
is the normal curvature of the surface in the ${\bf v}_1$ direction at this area
element. This normal curvature can be written as ${\bf v}_1^T S({\bf x}) {\bf v}_1$ where
$S({\bf x}) = \kappa_1 {\bf d}_1 \otimes {\bf d}_1 + \kappa_2 {\bf d}_2 \otimes {\bf d}_2$
is the *shape operator* at ${\bf x}$ expressed in terms of the surfaces'
principal curvatures and principal curvature directions.
The total bending energy in the homogenized inflated sheet for a
given direction field $\bf{v}_1$ on $\mathcal{M}$ is thus proportional to:
$$
\frac{1}{4} \int_\mathcal{M} ({\bf v}_1^T S {\bf v}_1)^2 \mathrm{d}A.
$$

We discretize the shape operator tensor field $S$ as a matrix stored on each triangle of our
target surface. For a given triangle, this matrix is the average of the
three corner vertices' shape operators, which in turn are constructed using `libigl`'s
quadric-fitting-based `principal_cuvature` function.

Adding this bending energy term to our original parameterization energy, we
arrive at the formulation:
$$
\begin{aligned}
E[f] := &\underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \int_\mathcal{M}
                    (\sigma_1 - 1)^2 + \left(\sigma_0 - \texttt{clamp}(\sigma_0, (\alpha_\text{min}, \pi / 2))\right)^2 \mathrm{d}A
        }_{\text{singular value fitting term}}
      + \underbrace{
            \frac{1}{4} \int_\mathcal{M} ({\bf v}_1^T S {\bf v}_1)^2 \mathrm{d}A
        }_{\text{bending regularization}},
 \\ &
      + \underbrace{
            \frac{w_\phi}{p_\phi} \sum_{i, j} \|{\bf u}_0^i \times {\bf u}_0^j\|^{p_\phi}
        }_{\text{direction regularization}}
      + \underbrace{
            \frac{w_\alpha}{p_\alpha} \sum_{i, j} |\sigma_0^i  - \sigma_0^j|^{p_\alpha}
        }_{\text{stretch regularization}}.
\end{aligned}
\label{eqn:regularized}\tag{3}
$$

## Results from Completely Unregularized Parametrization
Recall the unregularized parametrization formulation from @aharoni and its results for the Lilium surface:
$$
E[f] :=
\min_{U, V, \alpha} \frac{1}{2} \int_\mathcal{M} \! \left\| \nabla f -
    U
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \alpha & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    V^T
 \right\|_F^2 \ \mathrm{d}A.
\label{eqn:unregularized}\tag{4}
$$

[![](images/LocalGlobalLiliumPlot.png){width=800px}](images/LocalGlobalLiliumPlot.png){target=".blank"}

I originally thought that these unregularized results were too noisy to construct walls from:
my first attempts failed, giving thousands of small disconnected polygons instead of actual
walls. But it turns out that, by using a much higher resolution mesh for the stripe field
generation and wall extraction, I was able to generate walls after all:
![](images/noreg_stripe_field.png){width=400px}
![](images/noreg_walls.png){width=400px}

([Click here](data/lilium_noreg_walls.obj) to download an `obj` file containing the wall polylines.)

Surprisingly, these walls do a pretty good job of reproducing the surface, at least as
long as we constrain the boundary:
<figure>
<a href="3d_figures/lilium_noreg_fixed_bdry.html" target=".blank"><img src="images/lilium_noreg_fixed_bdry_compare.png" alt="Fixed boundary inflated structure for the unregularized air channel design." width="600" /></a>
<figcaption>Fixed boundary inflated structure for the unregularized air channel design (click for 3D view).</figcaption>
</figure>

If we free the boundary, the inflation deviates more from the target surface
than the bending-regularized design did.

</figure>

### Regularized vs Unregularized
The fairly good behavior of the unregularized design (especially compared to the
original smooth design in Figure 3) is apparently due to the less structured
channel orientations; this makes the straightening effects of the inflated
tubes less likely to accumulate to produce large changes to the shape encoded
in the metric. However, we should note that the regularized optimizations
(penalizing smoothness/tube bending) usually find parametrizations
achieving *lower* values for the unregularized fitting energy
$(\ref{eqn:unregularized})$ than the local-global iteration from @aharoni could.
In other words, the energy $(\ref{eqn:unregularized})$ does not in itself
prefer unstructured designs; these are picked arbitrarily and unpredictably by
the local-global iteration algorithm failing to converge to a good local
optimum. If we decide we want designs with less smooth orientations than we
get from $(\ref{eqn:regularized})$, we really need to formulate this goal in
the optimization/design space.

There are certainly issues with mostly straight/smoothly turning
tubes. When they saw the design in Figure 1, Emmanuel and Benoit also expressed concerns
about the straight channels being weak in bending. But there are
downsides to unstructured designs too. Here are some of the pros and cons I see of
the smoother bending-regularized designs found with $(\ref{eqn:regularized})$.

Pros: long, straight tubes look more elegant and are easier to mesh and fabricate. Specifically,
they can be meshed at a lower resolution, significantly accelerating the inflation simulation.
Fine-scale zig-zag designs likely will require meshes that are too large to simulate.
Having an initially smooth design probably also helps with the optimization: it is
more difficult to adjust a design with many sharp turns while still respecting
the fabrication constraints (bounds on the wall widths).

Cons: even when picking optimal alignments for mostly straight tubes, the
coherent straightening effects still accumulate to fight the curvature encoded
in the metric. And for umbilic surfaces like a half-sphere, all directions are
equally bad, and a zig-zag design would probably better prevent the unbending
effects from accumulating.

## Designing Zig-Zag Patterns
I think it is quite difficult to formulate a regularization term that encourages
a zig-zag structure at a particular length-scale (forcing channels to turn abruptly
if they have remained straight for "too long"). At least, I have not been able
to come up with anything like this yet.

The other approach is to design at a higher level, as originally suggested by Emmanuel and Benoit.
We could take the singular vector fields ${\bf u}_0$ and ${\bf u}_1$ found by a smooth
parametrization and use them to compute two orthogonal stripe fields, one aligned to ${\bf u}_0$ as in
Figure 1, and the other aligned to ${\bf u}_1$. Then we could use these two stripe fields as a periodic
2D coordinate system for placing a procedural 2D zig-zag pattern (you can view the current
[air channel construction](#air-channel-construction) procedure as using a periodic 1D coordinate
function--the single stripe field--for placing the channel walls). This 2D parametrization approach
is demonstrated in Figure 18 of @Knoppel2015.

## Next Steps
Apart from possibly exploring an explicit zig-zag design approach, the next
step is to run an optimization to improve the initial air channels generated
from the parametrization. To do this, we need to decide what
variables/representation to use for the optimization. For example, we could
directly optimize the wall vertex positions with a constraint to keep the walls
from inverting. Or we could try working with a smoother representation where
the walls are represented by spline curves (indicating the wall centers) and
thickness scalar fields defined on these curves.

Regardless of the representation we choose, the optimization problem will be
challenging because the total potential energy Hessian for the designs I've
shown is either not positive definite or barely positive definite at the
minimum energy configuration. In other words, there are some directions in which we can slightly perturb
the inflated vertex positions without changing the energy, so the equilibrium
configuration is not unique and cannot be considered a differentiable function
of the design variables. I believe this is due to the tension field theory
approximation we are using for the simulation, where compressive forces are
ignored.

This positive definiteness issue is problematic for the optimization
formulation I had in mind. I planned to express the optimization as minimizing
some objective function of the inflated configuration (e.g., its distance to the
target surface) with respect to the design parameters. Then each iteration of the
design optimization would involve solving for the current design's inflated
equilibrium and computing derivatives of the objective function with respect to
the design variables. This is the type of formulation I have used successfully
in the past (e.g., for our last  X-Shells Siggraph paper), but a singular or
indefinite potential energy Hessian means that these inner equilibrium solves will
be slow and the derivatives I compute may not be accurate.

Another formulation we might try is to have a single giant optimization with
both the design parameters and the inflated sheet's deformed configuration as
variables. We would minimize the same objective function as before, but we
would add an nonlinear equality constraint enforcing the equilibrium. This is a
more challenging/brute force and less elegant optimization problem, but it
avoids the need to solve for and differentiate equilibria at each iteration. We
could try using an augmented Lagrangian or SQP algorithm to solve this
optimization.
